Premises and equipment must be suitable for their intended pharmaceutical manufacturing
operations. Good Manufacturing Practice expects facility design, construction, maintenance and use
to minimize errors and contamination risks. Controls depend on the product,
process and manufacturing environment. This lesson introduces the principles rather than
prescribing one universal room design or classification.
Facility layout should support logical personnel and material movement and help
prevent contamination and mix-ups. Separate or appropriately controlled flows may be
necessary depending on the operation and risks. Material receipt, storage, dispensing,
production and dispatch each require suitable arrangements. The objective is controlled
movement and traceability, not simply a visually attractive floor plan.
Cleaning and housekeeping are essential routine controls. Cleaning procedures should specify
responsibilities, methods, materials and frequencies appropriate to the area or equipment.
Where necessary, cleaning effectiveness must be demonstrated and documented. Personnel should
promptly report spills, damage or abnormal conditions according to site procedures.
A clean appearance alone is not evidence that a cleaning process
is effective.
Manufacturing equipment should be appropriately designed, located and maintained for its
intended use. Product contact surfaces should be suitable for the materials
and processes involved. Equipment should allow effective cleaning and, where required,
sterilization. The level of control depends on criticality and intended function.
For example, a filling machine and a general office printer have
different GMP impacts.
Calibration establishes the relationship between an instrument indication and a reference
under specified conditions. Maintenance helps keep equipment in suitable operating condition.
Both should be planned, recorded and assessed for impact when overdue
or unsatisfactory. A calibration label is a useful visual control but
does not replace review of the applicable calibration record or equipment
status.
Qualification provides documented evidence that facilities, utilities and equipment are suitable
for their intended purpose. Installation qualification, operational qualification and performance qualification
are commonly described as I Q, O Q and P Q.
Their application and scope should follow a justified lifecycle and risk-based
approach. Acceptance criteria must be defined for the actual system and
process; there is no universal test limit for every item of
equipment.
Clear equipment identification and status controls help prevent unintended use. Site
procedures may use status labels, electronic systems, logbooks and approved records
to show equipment availability, maintenance, calibration, cleaning or qualification state. Operators
should verify status before use. If information is missing or inconsistent,
the discrepancy should be escalated rather than resolved by assumption.
Consider a vessel needed for a scheduled manufacturing batch. Its calibration
label indicates an expired due date, while the equipment logbook contains
no recent calibration entry. The operator should not assume the vessel
is acceptable. The finding should be reported, and authorized personnel should
assess instrument status, intended use and any potential product impact under
site procedures. Work should proceed only when the equipment is appropriately
released for use.
